title: Student-AI Interaction in an LLM-Empowered Learning Environment: A Cluster Analysis of Engagement Profiles
extended_summary:
This paper examines how university students engage with a large-language-model-powered learning environment and whether different patterns of student-AI interaction are associated with learning outcomes. The authors argue that simple counts of activity are insufficient to capture engagement in AI-supported learning, especially in multi-agent environments where students can interact with several pedagogical agents. Their research questions focus on how students engage with the course, what dialogue patterns characterize student interaction with AI agents, and how those patterns relate to learning and affective outcomes.

The intervention studied is a Massive AI-empowered Course (MAIC) system, an online platform that uses multiple LLM-based agents, including AI teachers, AI teaching assistants, AI student roles, and director agents that manage pacing and participation. Students took an eight-week introductory course on artificial general intelligence composed of six modules, with self-paced study, AI-supported dialogue, module quizzes, and pre/post testing. The study combined platform logs, coded dialogue data, questionnaires, and test scores. The authors used hierarchical cluster analysis to identify engagement profiles, LLM-assisted coding plus human review to classify dialogue by behavioral, cognitive, and emotional dimensions, and Epistemic Network Analysis to compare interaction structures across student groups.

Participants were 312 undergraduate students from a single elite university in China, with 110 completing the full course. The analyses identified two dropout profiles—early disengagers and stagnating interactors—and three completer profiles—survived lurkers, active questioners, and responsive navigators. Active questioners tended to ask questions and negotiate ideas, while responsive navigators showed more regulatory, responsive, and emotion-sharing behaviors. Lurkers completed the course with minimal interaction. Prior knowledge was associated with some interaction patterns and short-term quiz performance.

The main conclusion is that more interaction with AI does not automatically mean better engagement or better learning, and low interaction does not necessarily indicate poor outcomes. Students can benefit from AI-supported learning in different ways: some through active knowledge construction, others through regulation and navigation, and some through relatively independent learning with limited AI use. The paper concludes that multi-agent LLM learning environments can support personalized learning, but designers should recognize diverse engagement styles rather than assuming one ideal pattern of student-AI interaction.

identified_tools.name: MAIC
identified_tools.description: A Massive AI-empowered Course System: an online learning platform with multiple LLM-driven agents, including AI Teachers, AI Teaching Assistants, AI student personas, and director agents that coordinate instruction and responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as the primary learning environment for a six-module undergraduate introductory AI course, where 312 students viewed slides, interacted with multiple AI pedagogical agents, received instruction and real-time feedback, and completed quizzes/tests.

findings.finding_summary: Students showed distinct engagement profiles in MAIC: early disengagers (n=97), stagnating interactors (n=60), survived lurkers (n=75), and active completers (n=73). Controlling for pre-test, active completers achieved significantly higher average quiz scores (M=7.18, SD=1.23) than stagnating interactors (M=6.00, SD=1.63; t=2.84, p=.02) and lurkers (M=6.07, SD=1.40; t=3.23, p=.005), with ANCOVA F(2,125)=7.20, p=.001.
findings.measure: Average module quiz scores adjusted for pre-test

findings.finding_summary: Prior knowledge differed across engagement profiles: pre-test scores varied significantly across four clusters, F(3,127)=2.93, p=.04. Active completers scored higher on the pre-test (M=6.83, SD=1.61) than lurkers (M=5.96, SD=1.46), suggesting students with greater prior knowledge were more likely to engage actively in the MAIC environment.

Despite different interaction intensity, final course exam performance did not significantly differ between lurkers and active completers in MAIC. ANCOVA showed no significant difference between Cluster 3 and Cluster 4 on final exam scores, F(1,73)=3.53, p=.06, and no significant difference among Cluster 3 and the two active completer subclusters, F(2,72)=2.62, p=.08.

MAIC supported heterogeneous but successful participation patterns: 110 of 312 students completed the course, and the paper identified two dropout types and three completer types. The authors note this completion pattern compares favorably to typical MOOC completion rates, though no causal comparison group was used.
findings.measure: Course completion and engagement profile distribution

findings.finding_summary: Students’ attitudes toward AI increased after learning in MAIC for active completers, with a significant increase in Cluster 4 (z=2.31, p=.02) and a marginal increase in Cluster 3 (z=1.93, p=.05). No significant pre-post changes were found for motivation or academic self-efficacy, and between-cluster ANCOVA showed no significant differences in affective change outcomes.
findings.measure: Pre-post attitudes toward AI; motivation; academic self-efficacy questionnaires
findings.effect_size: z=2.31; z=1.93; Motivation F(2,104)=0.22; Academic Self-Efficacy F(2,104)=0.99; Attitudes toward AI F(2,104)=0.63

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used here for LLM-assisted coding of educational dialogue data.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as GPT-4o / GPT-4 Turbo to assist human coders in categorizing student-AI dialogue logs by behavioral, cognitive, and emotional codes.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic LLM-based pedagogical agents in a multi-agent learning environment providing instruction, Q&A, emotional support, and adaptive classroom orchestration.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied through students’ interactions with multiple unnamed/specialized AI agents (AI Teacher, AI Teaching Assistant, AI student personas, director agents) embedded in the course platform.

findings.finding_summary: Among highly interactive students, two dialogue-based engagement profiles emerged: active questioners (n=45) and responsive navigators (n=28). Active questioners showed significantly more asking questions (M=0.66 vs. 0.32, z=6.56, p<.001) and negotiating/confirming ideas (M=0.08 vs. 0.05, z=2.39, p=.02), while responsive navigators showed more responding to questions (M=0.07 vs. 0.01, z=4.15, p<.001), process regulation (M=0.15 vs. 0.07, z=2.02, p=.04), peer management (M=0.11 vs. 0.03, z=3.31, p<.001), and emotion sharing (M=0.07 vs. 0.02, z=4.07, p<.001).
findings.measure: Proportions of coded interaction behaviors in student-AI dialogues

findings.finding_summary: The two active interaction profiles achieved comparable learning outcomes in the multi-agent LLM environment. Average quiz scores were similar for active questioners (M=7.14, SD=1.27) and responsive navigators (M=7.26, SD=1.17), and final exam scores were also not significantly different among lurkers and the two active subclusters, F(2,72)=2.62, p=.08.
findings.measure: Average quiz scores and final exam scores by dialogue-based subcluster

findings.finding_summary: Prior knowledge was associated with interaction style within the LLM-based environment. Responsive navigators had higher pre-test scores (M=7.19, SD=1.68) than lurkers, t=3.21, p=.005, indicating prior knowledge significantly influenced interaction patterns and short-term learning benefits.

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical primary study with n=312, but it is observational/mixed-methods with clustering, dialogue coding, and associational analyses rather than an RCT or strong quasi-experimental design.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports statistically significant advantages for some engagement profiles on quiz outcomes and improved attitudes toward AI, but effect sizes are mostly not reported and key achievement outcomes such as final exam scores are null or mixed.
